claim: IP3R2 is co-expressed with GFAP in the hippocampus
source: In line with previous studies, we also found that IP3R2 was co-expressed with GFAP, but not bio-markers for microglia or neurons in the brain areas we tested including hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 demonstrating co-localization of IP3R2 with GFAP-positive astrocytes.

claim: IP3R2 is not expressed in microglia or neurons in the hippocampus
source: In line with previous studies, we also found that IP3R2 was co-expressed with GFAP, but not bio-markers for microglia or neurons in the brain areas we tested including hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing lack of co-localization between IP3R2 and markers for microglia (CX3CR1-GFP) or neurons.

claim: ATP-induced somatic Ca2+ elevation in astrocytes is abolished in Itpr2−/− mice in both VPm and hippocampus
source: Using Ca2+ imaging in acute brain slices, we next found that the ATP -induced somatic [Ca2+]i elevation in the astrocytes but not in the neurons of Itpr2−/− mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,c) was abolished in both of the VPm and hippocampus, confirming that Ca2+ signaling was selectively impaired in astrocytes in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,c demonstrating absence of ATP-induced calcium responses in astrocytes from Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: ATP-induced Ca2+ elevation in neurons is not affected in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Using Ca2+ imaging in acute brain slices, we next found that the ATP -induced somatic [Ca2+]i elevation in the astrocytes but not in the neurons of Itpr2−/− mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b,c) was abolished in both of the VPm and hippocampus, confirming that Ca2+ signaling was selectively impaired in astrocytes in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing preserved ATP-induced calcium responses in neurons from Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: The mean number of inputs received by each VPm neuron at P16-18 is significantly higher in Itpr2−/− mice compared to WT mice
source: Interestingly, we found a marked difference in the mean number of inputs received by each VPm neuron between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P16-18 (WT = 1.2 ± 0.02, n = 26 cells from 4 mice; Itpr2−/− = 2.1 ± 0.10, n = 40 cells from 6 mice; p<0.01, Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing quantified differences in input numbers between genotypes with statistical significance.

claim: Only 27% of VPm relay neurons in WT mice receive multiple Pr5 inputs at P16-18
source: In WT mice, only 27% (7 of 26) of VPm relay neurons received multiple Pr5 inputs at this age (Figure 1a,c), whereas most of these neurons (72%, 32 of 42) in Itpr2−/− mice received multiple Pr5 inputs (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing the distribution of input numbers across recorded neurons.

claim: 72% of VPm relay neurons in Itpr2−/− mice receive multiple Pr5 inputs at P16-18
source: In WT mice, only 27% (7 of 26) of VPm relay neurons received multiple Pr5 inputs at this age (Figure 1a,c), whereas most of these neurons (72%, 32 of 42) in Itpr2−/− mice received multiple Pr5 inputs (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing the distribution of input numbers across recorded neurons.

claim: VPm neurons receive two major excitatory inputs: one from layer VI cortex expressing VGluT1 and another from Pr5 expressing VGluT2
source: VPm relay neurons receive two major excitatory inputs: from layer VI cortex and the other from the Pr5 that express vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (VGluT1) and VGluT2, respectively (Graziano et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Graziano et al., 2008) establishing the anatomical organization of VPm inputs.

claim: There are more VGluT2 puncta around the soma in Itpr2−/− mice compared to WT mice at P16
source: Consistent with the electrophysiological results, we observed more VGluT2 puncta around the soma as well as the total numbers of puncta in Itpr2−/− mice (Figure 1e,f), indicating that there were more synapses in KO mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification of VGluT2 puncta shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Neuron number in the VPm does not significantly change between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P16-18
source: In addition, we found that neuron number did not significantly change in the VPm between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at this age (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of NeuN-positive neurons shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Astrocytic IP3R2-dependent Ca2+ signaling is required for synapse elimination
source: These results strongly suggested that astrocytic IP3R2-dependent Ca2+ signaling is required for synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined electrophysiological and immunohistochemical data showing impaired synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: Maximal AMPAR-EPSCs do not change between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P16
source: In this study, we did not find any change in maximal AMPAR-EPSCs, N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA-) EPSCs and APMAR-EPSC/NMDAR-EPSC ratios recorded at VPm relay synapses when WT mice were compared with Itpr2−/− at P16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of total input amplitudes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: NMDAR-EPSCs do not change between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P16
source: In this study, we did not find any change in maximal AMPAR-EPSCs, N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA-) EPSCs and APMAR-EPSC/NMDAR-EPSC ratios recorded at VPm relay synapses when WT mice were compared with Itpr2−/− at P16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: AMPAR-EPSC/NMDAR-EPSC ratios do not change between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P16
source: In this study, we did not find any change in maximal AMPAR-EPSCs, N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA-) EPSCs and APMAR-EPSC/NMDAR-EPSC ratios recorded at VPm relay synapses when WT mice were compared with Itpr2−/− at P16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4c.

claim: The strength of each input is weaker in Itpr2−/− mice compared to WT mice at P16
source: Given that the Itpr2−/− mice had more inputs and synapses, the strength of each input or individual synapse was weaker than that in WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing decreased average input amplitudes in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: The deficit of synapse elimination is sufficient to affect synaptic strengthening during development
source: These data revealed that the deficit of synapse elimination was sufficient to affect synaptic strengthening during development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that individual synapses are weaker in Itpr2−/− mice despite unchanged total synaptic strength.

claim: The number of inputs received by VPm neurons at P7 is comparable between WT and Itpr2−/− mice
source: We found that the number of inputs received by VPm neurons was comparable in the WT and Itpr2−/− mice (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings at P7 showing no significant difference in input numbers.

claim: The numbers of VGluT2 puncta per soma and per neuron do not differ between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P7
source: Neither the numbers of VGluT2 puncta per soma nor per neuron differed between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at this age, indicating similar numbers of synapses in these mice (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figure 2e,f.

claim: Synapse formation is normal at early postnatal stage in Itpr2−/− mice
source: These results suggested that synapse formation was normal at early postnatal stage in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that connectivity and synapse numbers are comparable between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P7.

claim: There are more Pr5-VPm synapses in Itpr2−/− mice than in WT mice at P30
source: We found that even at P30, there were more Pr5-VPm synapses in Itpr2−/− mice than in WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by VGluT2 immunostaining quantification at P30 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockout of IP3R2 disrupts developmental synapse elimination at the VPm relay synapses
source: Therefore, knockout of IP3R2 disrupted developmental synapse elimination at the VPm relay synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistent increase in synapse numbers in Itpr2−/− mice from P16 through P30.

claim: Basal ATP levels are reduced in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Among these gliotransmitters, we were particularly interested in ATP and assumed that it might play a role in synapse elimination for the following reasons: 1) the basal ATP levels are reduced in Itpr2−/− mice (Cao et al., 2013);
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Cao et al., 2013).

claim: Astrocytes release ATP in a Ca2+-dependent manner
source: Among these gliotransmitters, we were particularly interested in ATP and assumed that it might play a role in synapse elimination for the following reasons: 1) the basal ATP levels are reduced in Itpr2−/− mice (Cao et al., 2013); 2) astrocytes release ATP in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Lalo et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2007);
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lalo et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2007).

claim: ATP regulates synaptic plasticity
source: Among these gliotransmitters, we were particularly interested in ATP and assumed that it might play a role in synapse elimination for the following reasons: 1) the basal ATP levels are reduced in Itpr2−/− mice (Cao et al., 2013); 2) astrocytes release ATP in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Lalo et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2007); and 3) ATP regulates synaptic plasticity (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chen et al., 2013).

claim: A significant increase in basal ATP level occurs at P18 compared with P7 in WT mice
source: A significant increase in the basal ATP level occurred at P18 compared with that at P7 in WT mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The developmental up-regulation of basal ATP level is absent in Itpr2−/− mice
source: This developmental up-regulation of the basal ATP level was absent in Itpr2−/− mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements showing no increase from P7 to P18 in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: The basal ATP level is comparable between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P7
source: In addition, we found that the basal ATP level was comparable between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P7 but was significantly reduced in KO mice at P18 (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The basal ATP level is significantly reduced in Itpr2−/− mice compared to WT mice at P18
source: In addition, we found that the basal ATP level was comparable between WT and Itpr2−/− mice at P7 but was significantly reduced in KO mice at P18 (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of ATP from P11 to P15 rescues the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Next, we tested whether the deficit of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice could be rescued by compensatory ATP. To achieve this goal, we implanted a cannula in the left lateral ventricular of the brain (Figure 3b) and found that intracerebroventricular injection of ATP from P11 to P15 rescued the synapse elimination deficit (Figure 3e,i,l,m).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological and immunohistochemical data showing restoration of normal synapse elimination after ATP treatment.

claim: The majority of VPm neurons in Itpr2−/− mice that received ATP treatment are innervated by a single Pr5 input at P16-17
source: At P16-17, unlike aCSF-treated mice, the majority of VPm neurons in Itpr2−/− mice that had received ATP (50 µM) treatment was innervated by a single Pr5 input (Figure 3l).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing the distribution of input numbers after ATP treatment.

claim: The number of synapses significantly decreases in Itpr2−/− mice with ATP treatment
source: Immunostaining for VGluT2 also revealed that the number of synapses significantly decreased in Itpr2−/− mice with ATP treatment (Figure 3p,q).
evidence: The claim is supported by VGluT2 immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 3p,q.

claim: ATP treatment is sufficient to rescue synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice
source: These results indicate that ATP treatment is sufficient to rescue synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice and the removal of redundant synapses is independent of IP3R2-dependent Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of synapse elimination by exogenous ATP administration.

claim: The removal of redundant synapses is independent of IP3R2-dependent Ca2+ signaling
source: These results indicate that ATP treatment is sufficient to rescue synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice and the removal of redundant synapses is independent of IP3R2-dependent Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that exogenous ATP can rescue synapse elimination in the absence of IP3R2.

claim: Reactive astrocytes and activated microglia around the site of cannula placement are identical between aCSF and ATP treated-Itpr2−/− mice
source: We found that reactive astrocytes and activated microglia around the site of cannula placement in aCSF and ATP treated-Itpr2−/− mice were identical (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and ruled out this possibility.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification of GFAP and Iba1 staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low dose ATP (5 µM) cannot rescue impaired synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice
source: We next applied a low dose ATP (5 µM) and found that the impaired synapse elimination cannot be rescued in Itpr2−/− mice, suggesting the rescue effect of ATP was in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3n,o).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no rescue effect at low ATP concentration.

claim: The rescue effect of ATP is dose-dependent
source: We next applied a low dose ATP (5 µM) and found that the impaired synapse elimination cannot be rescued in Itpr2−/− mice, suggesting the rescue effect of ATP was in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3n,o).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of rescue effects at different ATP concentrations.

claim: ATPγS rescues the synapse elimination impairment in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Given that ATP is readily hydrolyzed, and to exclude the possibility that the degradation products of ATP play a role in synapse elimination, we injected the non-hydrolyzable ATP analog ATPγS and found that, ATPγS (50 µM) also rescued the synapse elimination impairment in Itpr2−/− mice (Figure 3f,j,l,m).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing rescue of synapse elimination with ATPγS treatment.

claim: Astrocytes mediate synapse elimination via Ca2+-dependent release of ATP
source: These results suggested that astrocytes mediate synapse elimination via the Ca2+-dependent release of ATP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue of synapse elimination by ATP and ATPγS in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of adenosine from P11 to P15 has no effect on Pr5-VPm connectivity at P16 in Itpr2−/− mice
source: We found intracerebroventricular injection of adenosine (50 µM) throughout P11-P15 had no effect on Pr5-VPm connectivity at P16 in these mice (Figure 3g, k, l, m).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no rescue effect with adenosine treatment.

claim: The synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice is rescued by ATP, but not adenosine
source: Thus, the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice was rescued by ATP, but not adenosine.
evidence: The claim is supported by the differential effects of ATP and adenosine treatments on synapse elimination.

claim: P2Y1 receptors are involved in ATP-induced heterosynaptic long-term depression in hippocampus
source: Particularly, P2Y1 receptors have been shown participated in ATP-induced heterosynaptic long-term depression (LTD) in hippocampus (Chen et al., 2013), and LTD has been suggested correlated to synapse elimination (Bastrikova et al., 2008; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chen et al., 2013; Bastrikova et al., 2008; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).

claim: LTD has been suggested to correlate with synapse elimination
source: Particularly, P2Y1 receptors have been shown participated in ATP-induced heterosynaptic long-term depression (LTD) in hippocampus (Chen et al., 2013), and LTD has been suggested correlated to synapse elimination (Bastrikova et al., 2008; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bastrikova et al., 2008; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).

claim: P2Y1 receptors are only expressed in neurons in the VPm
source: To test the possibility of involvement of P2Y1 receptors in synapse elimination at the VPm, we first examined the expression pattern of P2Y1 receptors and found that unlike in the hippocampus (Zhu and Kimelberg, 2004), they were only expressed in neurons in the VPm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 demonstrating P2Y1 expression in neurons but not astrocytes or microglia in VPm.

claim: ATP-induced somatic Ca2+ elevation in astrocytes is impaired in hippocampus but not in VPm in P2ry1−/− mice
source: We next found that ATP-induced somatic Ca2+ elevation in astrocytes was impaired in hippocampus, but not in the VPm in P2ry1−/− mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), further indicated that the expression pattern of P2Y1 receptors might be different in hippocampus when compared with that in the VPm.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATP-induced Ca2+ elevation in VPm neurons of P2ry1−/− mice is impaired
source: In line with immunostaining results, we also found that ATP-induced Ca2+ elevation in VPm neurons of P2ry1−/− mice was impaired (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of VPm neurons in P2ry1−/− mice receive multiple Pr5 inputs at P16
source: Compared to WT mice, the majority of VPm neurons in P2ry1−/− mice received multiple Pr5 inputs at P16 (WT = 30%, 13 of 33 cells; P2ry1−/− = 72%, 34 of 47 cells, Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing the distribution of input numbers.

claim: Synapse elimination is impaired in P2ry1−/− mice
source: Therefore, synapse elimination was also impaired in P2ry1−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiological and immunohistochemical data showing increased inputs and synapses in P2ry1−/− mice.

claim: There is more VGluT2 staining around the somata of VPm neurons in P2ry1−/− mice than in WT mice at P16
source: There was more VGluT2 staining around the somata of VPm neurons in P2ry1−/− mice than in WT mice (Figures 4i,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification shown in Figures 4i,j.

claim: The connectivity of Pr5-VPm pathway is comparable between WT and P2ry1−/− mice at P7
source: We found that the connectivity of Pr5-VPm pathway was comparable between WT and P2ry1−/− mice at P7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data at P7 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The synapse elimination deficit in P2ry1−/− mice is not rescued by intracerebroventricular injection of ATP from P11 to P15
source: In addition, the synapse elimination deficit in these mice was not rescued by intracerebroventricular injection of ATP from P11 to P15 (Figure 4c, f, g, h).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing no rescue effect of ATP in P2ry1−/− mice.

claim: Synapse elimination promoted by ATP depends on P2Y1 receptors
source: These results suggested that synapse elimination promoted by ATP may depend on P2Y1 receptors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ATP cannot rescue synapse elimination in P2ry1−/− mice.

claim: The deficit of synapse elimination is rescued by intracerebroventricular injection of MRS-2365 from P11 to P15 in Itpr2−/− mice
source: We next found that the deficit of synapse elimination was rescued by intracerebroventricular injection of a selective P2Y1 receptors agonist, MRS-2365 (20 µM) from P11 to P15 (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing rescue of synapse elimination with MRS-2365 treatment.

claim: The majority of VPm neurons in Itpr2−/− mice with treatment of MRS-2365 are innervated by a single Pr5 input
source: Unlike aCSF treatment, the majority of VPm neurons in Itpr2−/− mice with treatment of MRS-2365 innervated by a single Pr5 input (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing the distribution of input numbers after MRS-2365 treatment.

claim: The mean number of inputs received by each VPm neuron is significantly decreased in Itpr2−/− mice with intracerebroventricular injection of MRS-2365
source: The mean number of inputs received by each VPm neuron was significantly decreased in Itpr2−/− mice with intracerebroventricular injection of MRS-2365 (2.0 ± 0.76 MRS-2365 versus 1.33 ± 0.48 aCSF, Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological quantification shown in Figure 5d.

claim: ATP promotes synapse elimination via P2Y1 receptors
source: Taken together, these data confirmed that ATP promotes synapse elimination via P2Y1 receptors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results showing that P2Y1 agonist rescues synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice and ATP cannot rescue in P2ry1−/− mice.

claim: Astrocytes contribute to synapse elimination through Ca2+-dependent release of ATP and activation of P2Y1 receptors
source: Here, by using electrophysiological recording in transgenic mice, we found that astrocytes contribute to synapse elimination through Ca2+-dependent release of ATP and activation of P2Y1 receptors.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from the combined experimental results.

claim: Developmental synapse elimination in the VPm is impaired in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Specifically, we demonstrated that (1) developmental synapse elimination in the VPm was impaired in the Itpr2−/− mice;
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological and immunohistochemical data showing increased inputs and synapses in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of ATP and ATPγS, but not adenosine, from P11 to P15 rescues the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Specifically, we demonstrated that (1) developmental synapse elimination in the VPm was impaired in the Itpr2−/− mice; (2) intracerebroventricular injection of ATP and ATPγS, but not adenosine, from P11 to P15, rescued the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice;
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing differential rescue effects of ATP/ATPγS versus adenosine.

claim: P2ry1−/− mice show impaired synapse elimination that cannot be rescued by ATP
source: Specifically, we demonstrated that (1) developmental synapse elimination in the VPm was impaired in the Itpr2−/− mice; (2) intracerebroventricular injection of ATP and ATPγS, but not adenosine, from P11 to P15, rescued the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice; (3) P2ry1−/− mice also showed impaired synapse elimination and this could not be rescued by ATP;
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing impaired synapse elimination in P2ry1−/− mice and lack of rescue by ATP.

claim: Deficiency of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice is rescued by intracerebroventricular injection of MRS-2365 from P11 to P15
source: Specifically, we demonstrated that (1) developmental synapse elimination in the VPm was impaired in the Itpr2−/− mice; (2) intracerebroventricular injection of ATP and ATPγS, but not adenosine, from P11 to P15, rescued the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice; (3) P2ry1−/− mice also showed impaired synapse elimination and this could not be rescued by ATP; and (4) deficient of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice was rescued by intracerebroventricular injection of MRS-2365, a selective P2Y1 receptors agonist, from P11 to P15.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing rescue of synapse elimination with P2Y1 agonist treatment.

claim: Neurons make redundant synaptic connections early in development, and most inappropriate synapses are eliminated later to form precise neural circuitry
source: In the CNS, neurons make redundant synaptic connections early in development, and most of inappropriate synapses are eliminated later to form precise neural circuitry (Lichtman and Colman, 2000; Luo and O'Leary, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lichtman and Colman, 2000; Luo and O'Leary, 2005).

claim: Synapse elimination is believed to largely rely on neuronal activity
source: This process is believed to largely rely on neuronal activity, while the underlying mechanisms are still unclear.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus about activity-dependent synapse elimination.

claim: Astrocytes show a transient Ca2+ elevation in response to neuronal activity that depends on the GPCR/IP3R pathway
source: Recent studies have shown that astrocytes show a transient [Ca2+]i elevation, which depends on the GPCR/IP3R pathway, in response to neuronal activity and subsequently release gliotransmitters to modulate synaptic transmission and plasticity (Araque et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Araque et al., 2014).

claim: Astrocytic Ca2+ elevation is a consequence of neuronal activity
source: Therefore, astrocytic [Ca2+]i elevation is a consequence of neuronal activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that neuronal activity triggers astrocytic calcium responses.

claim: Activity-dependent competition for synapse elimination involves both postsynaptic neuronal activation and astrocytic Ca2+ elevation
source: Based on these reasons, we proposed that activity-dependent competition for synapse elimination involves both postsynaptic neuronal activation and astrocytic [Ca2+]I elevation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their reasoning.

claim: GPCR/IP3R-dependent Ca2+ signaling is critical for astrocytes to release gliotransmitters and modulate synaptic transmission
source: A large literature has shown that GPCR/IP3R-dependent Ca2+ signaling is critical for astrocytes to release gliotransmitters and modulate synaptic transmission.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus from multiple studies.

claim: IP3R2-mediated Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes may not be involved in the acute modulation of neuronal activity and synaptic transmission
source: Conversely, recent studies from McCarthy's laboratory have suggested that IP3R2-mediated Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes may not be involved in the acute modulation of neuronal activity and synaptic transmission (Fiacco et al., 2007; Petravicz et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Fiacco et al., 2007; Petravicz et al., 2008).

claim: There are still some Ca2+ fluctuations occurring in astrocyte processes in Itpr2−/− mice, although somatic Ca2+ signaling is eliminated
source: Two studies have shown that there were still some Ca2+ fluctuations occurring in astrocytes process, although the somatic Ca2+ signaling was eliminated in Itpr2−/− mice (Kanemaru et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kanemaru et al., 2014; Srinivasan et al., 2015).

claim: Ca2+ signaling is not totally removed in Itpr2−/− mice
source: These results suggested that Ca2+ signaling was not totally removed in these mutants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from studies showing residual Ca2+ signaling in astrocyte processes of Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: Astrocytic IP3R2-dependent somatic Ca2+ signaling is required for developmental synapse elimination
source: Our studies strongly suggested that astrocytic IP3R2-dependent somatic Ca2+ signaling is required for developmental synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Astrocytic Ca2+ signaling in the process and soma may play different roles in gliotransmitter release and regulating neuronal functions
source: Considering the dynamic and complexity, the astrocytic Ca2+ signaling in the process and the soma may play different roles in gliotransmitter release and regulating neuronal functions (Volterra et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citation to previous literature (Volterra et al., 2014).

claim: Synapse elimination is only partly impaired in Itpr2−/− and P2ry1−/− mice
source: It is important to note that synapse elimination was only partly impaired in the Itpr2−/− and P2ry1−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that some degree of synaptic pruning still occurs in the mutant mice.

claim: Some degree of synaptic pruning still occurs during P7 to P16 in Itpr2−/− and P2ry1−/− mice
source: Although we found both anatomical and electrophysiological evidence that these mice had significant deficits in developmental synapse elimination, some degree of synaptic pruning still occurred during P7 to P16, suggesting that there are multiple mechanisms for controlling synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that input numbers decrease from P7 to P16 even in mutant mice.

claim: There are multiple mechanisms for controlling synapse elimination
source: Although we found both anatomical and electrophysiological evidence that these mice had significant deficits in developmental synapse elimination, some degree of synaptic pruning still occurred during P7 to P16, suggesting that there are multiple mechanisms for controlling synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the partial impairment of synapse elimination in the mutant mice.

claim: Synaptic pruning in the VPm relay synapses occurs at several developmental stages
source: Indeed, synaptic pruning in the VPm relay synapses occurs at several developmental stages (Wang and Zhang, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Wang and Zhang, 2008).

claim: Before P10, pruning is insensitive to whisker deprivation
source: Before P10, pruning is insensitive to whisker deprivation, but then later, the elimination of redundant inputs is largely dependent on somatosensory experience.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about developmental stages of synapse elimination.

claim: After P10, the elimination of redundant inputs is largely dependent on somatosensory experience
source: Before P10, pruning is insensitive to whisker deprivation, but then later, the elimination of redundant inputs is largely dependent on somatosensory experience.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about developmental stages of synapse elimination.

claim: The connectivity between Pr5 and VPm in Itpr2−/− mice undergone ATP and ATPγS treatments restores to WT mice level
source: We found surprisingly, the connectivity between Pr5 and VPm in Itpr2−/− mice undergone ATP and ATPγS treatments restored to WT mice level.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing complete rescue of synapse elimination with ATP/ATPγS treatment.

claim: ATP is sufficient to rescue the impairment of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice regardless of whether sensory information has been changed
source: These results suggested that no matter sensory information had been changed or not, ATP was sufficient to rescue the impairment of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the complete rescue of synapse elimination by ATP treatment.

claim: Mice open their eyes and start to use their vibrissae to explore the environment at about P13
source: It is about P13 that mice open their eyes and start to use their vibrissae to explore the environment.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about mouse development.

claim: There is a significant enhancement of the basal ATP level in the VPm of WT mice between P7 and P18
source: Accompanying this behavioral change, we found a significant enhancement of the basal ATP level in the VPm of WT mice between P7 and P18 (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The basal ATP level fails to be up-regulated in Itpr2−/− mice during development
source: However, the basal ATP level failed to be up-regulated in Itpr2−/− mice during development.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements showing no developmental increase in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: ATP can be released by both neurons and glia
source: ATP can be released by both neurons and glia.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific knowledge.

claim: The decreased ATP level in Itpr2−/− mice is most likely due to astrocytes since IP3R2 is not expressed in neurons
source: The decreased ATP level in Itpr2−/− mice was most likely due to astrocytes since IP3R2 was not expressed in neurons and [Ca2+]i elevation did not change in neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cell-type specific expression of IP3R2 and preserved neuronal calcium signaling.

claim: Adenosine is a ligand for adenosine receptors and causes synaptic depression
source: Although ATP itself is a signaling molecule by activating P2X or P2Y receptors, the degraded form adenosine is also a ligand for adenosine receptors and causes synaptic depression (Wu and Saggau, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Wu and Saggau, 1994).

claim: Adenosine injection through P11-15 does not rescue the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice, excluding a role for adenosine in synapse elimination
source: The fact that adenosine injection through P11-15 did not rescue the synapse elimination deficit in Itpr2−/− mice excludes the possibility of a role for adenosine in synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of rescue effect with adenosine treatment.

claim: ATP is an energy currency in the brain
source: In addition to being a signal molecule, ATP is also energy currency in the brain and the phenotype of Itpr2−/− mice could be a result of global metabolic stress.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific knowledge about ATP function.

claim: The phenotype of Itpr2−/− mice is not a result of global metabolic stress
source: This possibility is very unlikely because either ATPγS, a non-hydrolyzable ATP analog or one selective P2Y1 receptors agonist MRS-2365 could rescue the deficit of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue effects of non-metabolizable ATP analogs and P2Y1 agonists.

claim: ATP is not acting as an energy supply to play a role in synapse elimination
source: In our study, we concluded that ATP was not acting as an energy supply to play a role in synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is concluded from the rescue effects of non-hydrolyzable ATP analogs.

claim: P2Y1 receptors are widely expressed in astrocytes, microglia and neurons
source: Unlike IP3R2, studies have shown that P2Y1 receptors are widely expressed in astrocytes, microglia and neurons.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Loss of function of P2Y1 receptors in all three cell types may contribute to impaired synapse elimination in P2ry1−/− mice
source: Thus, loss function of P2Y1 receptors in all three types of cell may contribute to the phenomenon of impaired synapse elimination in P2ry1−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the cellular mechanisms underlying the phenotype.

claim: P2Y1 receptors are expressed by astrocytes
source: First, P2Y1 receptors have been shown to be expressed by astrocytes (Pascual et al., 2012), therefore the finding that P2ry1−/− mice has impaired synapse elimination could be due to a failure to increase calcium levels in astrocytes in response to ATP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Pascual et al., 2012).

claim: Astrocytes in the VPm of P2ry1−/− mice respond to ATP with a similar increase in intracellular Ca2+ compared to WT mice
source: This possibility could be excluded by the results of astrocytes in the VPm of P2ry1-/- mice responded to ATP with a similar increase in intracellular Ca2+ when compared to cells in the WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: P2Y1 receptors are not expressed by astrocytes in the VPm
source: Additionally, we found that P2Y1 receptors were not expressed by astrocytes in the VPm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), but abundantly expressed in the hippocampus astrocytes (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: P2Y1 receptors are abundantly expressed in hippocampus astrocytes
source: Additionally, we found that P2Y1 receptors were not expressed by astrocytes in the VPm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), but abundantly expressed in the hippocampus astrocytes (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished data mentioned by the authors.

claim: P2Y1 receptors have been reported to be expressed in microglia
source: Second, P2Y1 receptors have been reported to be expressed in microglia and ATP activates microglia.
evidence: The claim reflects knowledge from previous literature.

claim: There is little protein evidence for P2Y1 receptor expression on microglia
source: At present, there were some mRNA and functional clues showing that microglia expressed P2Y1 receptors, whereas the protein evidence was very few (Fields and Burnstock, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fields and Burnstock, 2006).

claim: No P2Y1 protein expression was found on microglia in both hippocampus and VPm
source: In our study, we did not find any P2Y1 protein expression on microglia in both of hippocampus (data not shown) and the VPm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The protein level of P2Y1 receptors expressed on microglia in the VPm is very low
source: Therefore, the protein level of P2Y1 receptors expressed on microglia in the VPm, if any, was very low.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of detectable P2Y1 protein on microglia.

claim: ATP-mediated synapse elimination most likely occurs through activation of neuronal P2Y1 receptors
source: Last, ATP-mediates synapse elimination may occur through activation of neuronal P2Y1 receptors. This speculation is most likely due to P2Y1 receptors are abundantly expressed in VPm neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the expression pattern of P2Y1 receptors and functional data.

claim: P2Y1 receptors are abundantly expressed in VPm neurons
source: Last, ATP-mediates synapse elimination may occur through activation of neuronal P2Y1 receptors. This speculation is most likely due to P2Y1 receptors are abundantly expressed in VPm neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: ATP-evoked Ca2+ response in VPm neurons is significantly decreased in P2ry1−/− mice
source: In addition, our Ca2+ imaging data showing that ATP-evoked Ca2+ response in VPm neurons was significantly decreased in P2ry1-/- mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: ATP may activate neuronal P2Y1 receptors to promote synapse elimination
source: Our findings strongly suggest that ATP may activate neuronal P2Y1 receptors to promote synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the expression pattern and functional data.

claim: Activation of neuronal P2Y1 receptors is required for astrocyte-derived ATP mediated LTD in hippocampus
source: This hypothesis is supported by a previous study showing that activation of neuronal P2Y1 receptors is required for astrocytes derived ATP mediated LTD in hippocampus (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Chen et al., 2013).

claim: There is a close linkage between LTD and synapse elimination
source: Due to a close linkage proposed between LTD and synapse elimination (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013), one possible model is that ATP and downstream purinergic signaling could recognize unwanted synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013).

claim: ATP and downstream purinergic signaling could recognize unwanted synapses
source: Due to a close linkage proposed between LTD and synapse elimination (Wiegert and Oertner, 2013), one possible model is that ATP and downstream purinergic signaling could recognize unwanted synapses.
evidence: The claim is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Selective elimination of unwanted synapses is vital for the precise formation of neuronal circuits during development
source: Selective elimination of unwanted synapses is vital for the precise formation of neuronal circuits during development, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of synapse elimination remain unclear
source: Selective elimination of unwanted synapses is vital for the precise formation of neuronal circuits during development, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: The claim reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of ATP, but not adenosine, rescued the deficit in synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice
source: Interestingly, intracerebroventricular injection of ATP, but not adenosine, rescued the deficit in synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential rescue effects.

claim: Developmental synapse elimination is impaired in P2ry1−/− mice and is not rescued by ATP
source: Further studies showed that developmental synapse elimination was also impaired in P2ry1−/− mice and was not rescued by ATP, indicating a possible role of purinergic signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in P2ry1−/− mice.

claim: MRS-2365, a selective P2Y1 agonist, can rescue the deficit of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice
source: This hypothesis was confirmed by MRS-2365, a selective P2Y1 agonist, could also rescue the deficient of synapse elimination in Itpr2−/− mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue with P2Y1 agonist.

claim: Astrocytes release ATP in an IP3R2-dependent manner to regulate synapse elimination
source: Our results uncovered a novel mechanism suggesting that astrocytes release ATP in an IP3R2-dependent manner to regulate synapse elimination.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental results.

claim: Activity-dependent competition among different inputs is a key mechanism for synapse elimination
source: Although activity-dependent competition among different inputs has been suggested as the key mechanisms for synapse elimination, the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus.

claim: Disruption of synapse elimination is likely involved in neurological diseases such as schizophrenia and autism
source: Disruption of this process is likely involved in many neurological diseases such as schizophrenia and autism (Hoffman and McGlashan, 1997; Tang et al., 2014; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Hoffman and McGlashan, 1997; Tang et al., 2014; Tsai et al., 2012).

claim: The Pr5-VPm connection in mice is an excellent model to investigate developmental synapse elimination in the CNS
source: In addition to the retino-geniculate and climbing fiber-Purkinje cell pathways (Chen and Regehr, 2000; Kano and Hashimoto, 2009), the principal trigeminal nucleus-ventral posteriormedial thalamic nucleus (Pr5-VPm) connection in mice has proven to be an excellent model in which to investigate developmental synapse elimination in the central nervous system (Arsenault and Zhang, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chen and Regehr, 2000; Kano and Hashimoto, 2009; Arsenault and Zhang, 2006).

claim: VPm neurons receive a contralateral Pr5 projection and relay information to the somatosensory cortex
source: VPm neurons receive a contra-lateral Pr5 projection and relay the information to the somatosensory cortex.
evidence: The claim reflects established anatomical knowledge.

claim: At P7, each VPm neuron receives an average of 7-8 Pr5 inputs
source: At an early age like postnatal day 7 (P7), each VPm neuron receives an average of 7–8 Pr5 inputs.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about developmental connectivity.

claim: Most Pr5 inputs are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner during development
source: Most of these inputs are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner during development and the majority of VPm neurons only receive a single Pr5 input by P16.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about developmental synapse elimination.

claim: The majority of VPm neurons only receive a single Pr5 input by P16
source: Most of these inputs are eliminated in an activity-dependent manner during development and the majority of VPm neurons only receive a single Pr5 input by P16.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about developmental connectivity.

claim: Astrocytes contact 50-90% of synapses in a given brain region
source: Structurally, astrocytes contact 50–90% of the synapses in a given brain region (Genoud et al., 2006; Oliet et al., 2001) and form one component of the "tripartite synapse" (Araque et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Genoud et al., 2006; Oliet et al., 2001).

claim: Astrocytes form one component of the tripartite synapse
source: Structurally, astrocytes contact 50–90% of the synapses in a given brain region (Genoud et al., 2006; Oliet et al., 2001) and form one component of the "tripartite synapse" (Araque et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Araque et al., 1999).

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ elevation in astrocytes can be induced by activation of synapses
source: Functionally, intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) elevation in neighboring astrocytes can be induced by activation of the synapse, triggering the release of gliotransmitters such as ATP and D-serine that modulate synaptic efficacy and plasticity (Chen et al., 2013; Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Henneberger et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Astrocytes release gliotransmitters such as ATP and D-serine that modulate synaptic efficacy and plasticity
source: Functionally, intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i) elevation in neighboring astrocytes can be induced by activation of the synapse, triggering the release of gliotransmitters such as ATP and D-serine that modulate synaptic efficacy and plasticity (Chen et al., 2013; Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Henneberger et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Chen et al., 2013; Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Henneberger et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2003).

claim: Astrocytes release gliotransmitters in a GPCR/IP3R-mediated Ca2+-dependent manner
source: It is generally accepted that astrocytes release gliotransmitters in a G-protein-coupled receptor/ inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (GPCR/IP3R)-mediated Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim reflects established scientific consensus.

claim: GPCR-mediated Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes depends on the activation of IP3R2 in response to neuronal activity
source: Studies in both acute slice preparations and in vivo have shown that, in response to neuronal activity, GPCR-mediated Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes depends on the activation of IP3R2, a subunit that is solely expressed in astrocytes (Fiacco and McCarthy, 2004; Navarrete et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Fiacco and McCarthy, 2004; Navarrete et al., 2012).

claim: IP3R2 is a subunit that is solely expressed in astrocytes
source: Studies in both acute slice preparations and in vivo have shown that, in response to neuronal activity, GPCR-mediated Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes depends on the activation of IP3R2, a subunit that is solely expressed in astrocytes (Fiacco and McCarthy, 2004; Navarrete et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Fiacco and McCarthy, 2004; Navarrete et al., 2012).

claim: There are other Ca2+ signaling pathways in astrocytes which do not involve IP3R2
source: Indeed, there are other Ca2+ signaling pathways in astrocytes which do not involve IP3R2.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about astrocyte calcium signaling diversity.

claim: Somatic Ca2+ signaling is eliminated in astrocytes of Itpr2−/− mice, but Ca2+ signaling in processes is intact
source: A recent study showed that although the somatic Ca2+ signaling was eliminated, Ca2+ signaling in processes was intact in the astrocyes of Itpr2−/− mice (Srinivasan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Srinivasan et al., 2015).

claim: IP3-induced Ca2+ increase is the major source for somatic Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes
source: Therefore, IP3-induced Ca2+ increase is only the major source for somatic Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from studies showing elimination of somatic but not process calcium signaling in Itpr2−/− mice.

claim: Astrocytes mediate synapse elimination in a neuronal activity-dependent manner through phagocytosis via MEGF10 and MERTK pathways
source: Recent studies have shown that astrocytes could mediate synapse elimination in a neuronal activity-dependent manner through two distinct pathways: either directly by phagocytosis through the MEGF10 and MERTK pathways, or by activating the classical complement cascade via astrocyte-derived transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) (Bialas and Stevens, 2013; Chung et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bialas and Stevens, 2013; Chung et al., 2013).

claim: Astrocytes mediate synapse elimination by activating the classical complement cascade via astrocyte-derived TGF-β
source: Recent studies have shown that astrocytes could mediate synapse elimination in a neuronal activity-dependent manner through two distinct pathways: either directly by phagocytosis through the MEGF10 and MERTK pathways, or by activating the classical complement cascade via astrocyte-derived transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) (Bialas and Stevens, 2013; Chung et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bialas and Stevens, 2013; Chung et al., 2013).

claim: Ca2+-permeable AMPARs in Bergmann glia are required for developmental elimination of climbing fiber-Purkinje cell inputs
source: The results from studies in the cerebellum suggested that Ca2+-permeableα-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors (AMPARs) in Bergmann glia are required for the developmental elimination of climbing fiber-Purkinje cell inputs, which provides a clue that astrocytic Ca2+ signaling might be involved in synapse elimination (Iino et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Iino et al., 2001).

claim: Bergmann glia are morphologically distinct from astrocytes
source: Unfortunately, it is difficult to draw an exclusive conclusion since Bergmann glia are morphologically distinct from astrocytes and detect synaptic activity at cerebellar synapses primarily though activation of Ca2+-permeable AMPARs as well as GPCRs.
evidence: The claim reflects established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Bergmann glia detect synaptic activity at cerebellar synapses primarily through activation of Ca2+-permeable AMPARs and GPCRs
source: Unfortunately, it is difficult to draw an exclusive conclusion since Bergmann glia are morphologically distinct from astrocytes and detect synaptic activity at cerebellar synapses primarily though activation of Ca2+-permeable AMPARs as well as GPCRs.
evidence: The claim reflects established knowledge about Bergmann glia function.
